claim: Meta3C allows characterizing individual genomes and their average organization within a mix of organisms.
source: Using controlled mixes of bacterial and yeast species, we developed meta3C, a metagenomic chromosome conformation capture approach that allows characterizing individual genomes and their average organization within a mix of organisms.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental results presented throughout the manuscript, including contact maps and 3D reconstructions of multiple species from mixed populations.

claim: A single meta3C library can be used for assembling, scaffolding and characterizing the tridimensional organization of unknown genomes.
source: Not only can meta3C be applied to species already sequenced, but a single meta3C library can be used for assembling, scaffolding and characterizing the tridimensional organization of unknown genomes.
evidence: This is demonstrated through the de novo assembly and scaffolding experiments on bacterial and yeast mixtures described in the Results section.

claim: The E. coli HB101 strain used in the analysis contains a F' plasmid carrying a ~140 kb duplicated region of the E. coli chromosome.
source: We first noticed that a large (∼140 kb) region of the E. coli genome exhibited a two fold increase of the read coverage, indicating a segmental duplication. This region was also enriched in contacts with the F plasmid sequence (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,B), prompting us to hypothesize that one of the two copy was actually carried by a F' plasmid (i.e., a F plasmid carrying bacterial sequences).
evidence: This hypothesis is supported by read coverage data, contact frequency analysis, and confirmed by Southern blot experiments.

claim: The F' plasmid is positioned preferentially in the vicinity of the replication origin (Ori) and termination (Ter) regions in fast growing E. coli cells.
source: Interestingly, besides this duplication, two regions along the E. coli chromosome appeared enriched in contacts with the F' plasmid: the replication origin (Ori) and, to a lower extent, the termination (Ter) regions (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B). This indicates that the F' plasmid is positioned preferentially in the vicinity of these regions in fast growing cells, as expected given the preferred location of the F plasmid in mid, 1/4, and 3/4 positions in the cell, which are also preferred positions for Ori/Ter regions during the cell cycle (Gordon et al., 1997; Niki and Hiraga, 1997).
evidence: This is based on contact frequency data and supported by literature citations about F plasmid positioning.

claim: The replichores of B. subtilis and V. cholerae exhibit global symmetry visible as a counter-diagonal in the contact map.
source: In B. subtilis and V. cholerae this symmetry was made clearly visible, in the growth conditions used in this experiment, by the presence of a counter-diagonal in the map (running opposite to the continuous and strong signal that accounts for the contact between adjacent DNA segments; see also the correlation version of the contact map on Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is directly observed in the contact maps shown in Figure 1.

claim: The global symmetry and counter-diagonal pattern in bacterial chromosomes reflects a longitudinal organization of the two replichores extending along parallel axes within the cell.
source: This global symmetry as well as this second opposite diagonal, reflecting a longitudinal organization of the two replichores extending along parallel axes within the cell, were also reported for Caulobacter crescentus (Umbarger et al., 2011; Le et al., 2013).
evidence: This interpretation is supported by comparison with published studies on C. crescentus.

claim: The E. coli chromosome exhibits an open 3D structure with no visible diagonal in the contact matrix.
source: The two arms of the E. coli chromosome exhibited an open 3D structure, with no visible diagonal in the matrix.
evidence: This is observed in the contact map and 3D reconstruction shown in Figure 1.

claim: B. subtilis has a relatively compact domain at the Ori region that overlaps with the region containing centromere-like parS sites.
source: The 3D reconstruction of the B. subtilis genome revealed a relatively compact domain at the Ori region that overlapped with the region of the genome containing the centromere-like parS sites, in agreement with the structural role described for the ParS/Spo0J/Smc complex in the literature (Gruber and Errington, 2009; Sullivan et al., 2009).
evidence: This is observed in the 3D reconstruction and supported by literature on the ParS/Spo0J/Smc complex.

claim: The E. coli chromosome presents a strong Ter domain that exhibits fewer contacts with the rest of the genome, reflecting the structuring role of the MatP/matS system.
source: By contrast, the E. coli chromosome presented a strong Ter domain that was clearly identifiable in the contact map and exhibited fewer contacts with the rest of the genome, reflecting most likely the structuring role of the MatP/matS system (Mercier et al., 2008).
evidence: This is observed in the contact map and interpreted based on literature about the MatP/matS system.

claim: In V. cholerae, the Ter regions of chromosomes 1 and 2 are in closer proximity than the two Ori regions.
source: For V. cholerae, the Ter regions of chromosomes 1 and 2 were in closer proximity than the two Ori regions, reflecting the controlled segregation mechanisms of these two unequal-sized chromosomes (Val et al., 2008).
evidence: This is observed in the 3D reconstruction and contact map, and interpreted based on literature about V. cholerae chromosome segregation.

claim: V. cholerae chromosomes I and II achieve replication synchronously at their termination regions.
source: Whereas the two Ter regions appeared of the same color, consistent with the fact that both chromosomes I and II achieve replication synchronously (Rasmussen et al., 2007), the Ori regions presented, as expected, different coverages: chromosome I initiates replication first whereas chromosome II starts only to replicate later.
evidence: This is inferred from read coverage data and supported by a citation about V. cholerae replication timing.

claim: The meta3C library of three bacteria contains approximately 80% regular paired-end reads.
source: This relatively high percentage results from the fact that, unlike the Hi-C protocol (Lieberman-Aiden et al., 2009), meta3C does not involve an enrichment step for religated fragments ('Materials and methods').
evidence: This is stated as a characteristic of the meta3C protocol compared to Hi-C.

claim: De novo assembly of the three bacterial meta3C library generated 2,436 contigs with N50 = 55 kb and total length 12.5 Mb.
source: Using the assembly program IDBA-UD (Peng et al., 2012), a set of 2,436 contigs was generated from the 3C read pairs (N50 = 55 kb, total length 12.5 Mb).
evidence: This is a direct result from the assembly analysis.

claim: The assembled contigs from the bacterial meta3C library covered 96%, 98%, and 93% of the V. cholerae, E. coli, and B. subtilis reference genomes, respectively.
source: The quality of these contigs was assessed by comparing them with published reference genomes, which showed that the assembled contigs covered respectively 96%, 98%, and 93% of the V. cholerae, E. coli, and B. subtilis reference genomes and that only 0.7% of the contigs (52,373 bp total) were chimeric.
evidence: This is a quantitative assessment of assembly quality by comparison to reference genomes.

claim: Only 0.7% of the contigs from the bacterial meta3C assembly were chimeric.
source: The quality of these contigs was assessed by comparing them with published reference genomes, which showed that the assembled contigs covered respectively 96%, 98%, and 93% of the V. cholerae, E. coli, and B. subtilis reference genomes and that only 0.7% of the contigs (52,373 bp total) were chimeric.
evidence: This is a quantitative assessment of assembly quality.

claim: The Louvain algorithm successfully clustered contigs from the bacterial meta3C assembly into three communities, each corresponding to a different species.
source: The meta3C reads were then realigned on the de novo contigs and the contact information was used to pool the contigs into communities sharing similar contact behavior (hence likely belonging to the same genome) using the Louvain algorithm (Blondel et al., 2008). Three communities of contigs were generated, each corresponding to a different species and covering respectively 96, 98, and 92% of the genomes of V. cholerae, E. coli, and B. subtilis, respectively (Figure 1E).
evidence: This demonstrates the effectiveness of using contact information for binning contigs by species.

claim: The Rabl configuration with co-localized centromeres is the primary driver of yeast genome organization.
source: In contrast to the diversity of structures observed for the bacterial species analyzed above, the Rabl configuration appeared as the primary driver of yeast genome organization, as illustrated by the individual 3D structures of the genomes of Yarrowia lipolytica and Naumovozyma castellii (Figure 2C, Animation 8,9).
evidence: This is observed in the contact maps and 3D reconstructions of multiple yeast species.

claim: De novo assembly of the 11 yeast species mixture generated contigs with N50 = 6,914 bp and total length 138 Mb.
source: To test the potential of using meta3C reads for assembling de novo such a complex mix of yeast genomes, we assembled them using IDBA-UD (N50 = 6,914 bp, total length 138 Mb).
evidence: This is a direct result from the assembly analysis.

claim: The breadth of coverage of the 11 yeast genomes by assembled contigs ranged from 89.8% (Candida albicans) to 98.3% (N. castellii).
source: The breadth of coverage of the 11 genomes by the resulting contigs ranged from 89.8% (Candida albicans) to 98.3% (N. castellii), with chimeric contigs (misassemblies) representing ∼20% of the total (37 Mb).
evidence: This is a quantitative assessment of assembly quality for the yeast mixture.

claim: Chimeric contigs in the yeast assembly represented approximately 20% of the total (37 Mb).
source: The breadth of coverage of the 11 genomes by the resulting contigs ranged from 89.8% (Candida albicans) to 98.3% (N. castellii), with chimeric contigs (misassemblies) representing ∼20% of the total (37 Mb).
evidence: This is a quantitative assessment of assembly quality.

claim: The high percentage of chimeric contigs in the yeast assembly is caused by frequent occurrence of identical or near-identical genome regions such as transposable elements, not by intergenomic 3C paired-end reads.
source: To monitor the influence of chimeric pairs of reads (originating from intergenomic 3D contacts) on the generation of chimeric contigs, we performed an assembly on the same library using the Velvet software that considers all reads as independents (i.e., without pairing them; Zerbino and Birney, 2008). This assembly exhibited a dramatic increase (73%, 69 Mb) in chimeric contigs, demonstrating that these misassemblies were not caused by intergenomic 3C paired-end reads but rather by the frequent occurrence of identical or near-identical genome regions (such as transposable elements) in those eukaryotic genomes.
evidence: This conclusion is based on a comparative assembly experiment using Velvet.

claim: The Louvain algorithm clustered the yeast contigs into 13 sub-groups: one for each of the 11 yeast species, one for an E. coli contaminant, and one for mitochondrial genome fragments.
source: The clustering procedure resulted in 13 sub-groups: one for each of the 11 yeast species, one corresponding to an E. coli contaminant, and one comprising various misassembled fragments of mitochondrial genomes. In total, only 1% of the assembly (2% of the contigs) could not be attributed to a given species (Figure 2D).
evidence: This demonstrates the effectiveness of the clustering approach for the yeast mixture.

claim: Only 1% of the yeast assembly (2% of the contigs) could not be attributed to a given species.
source: In total, only 1% of the assembly (2% of the contigs) could not be attributed to a given species (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is a quantitative measure of the clustering success.

claim: GRAAL scaffolding of N. castellii contigs from the yeast mixture resulted in 11 superscaffolds covering 94.5% of the reference sequence of the 10 chromosomes.
source: Overall these 11 scaffolds covered 94.5% of the reference sequence of the 10 chromosomes (chromosome 3 was split into two scaffolds because of the presence of the large, unassembled rDNA array on this chromosome), illustrating the ability of this de novo analysis to correctly assemble and scaffold unknown genomes (see Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This demonstrates the effectiveness of GRAAL for scaffolding from meta3C data.

claim: GRAAL processing breaks chimeric contigs into non-chimeric parts, thereby correcting assembly errors.
source: Since this algorithm involves a splitting procedure of the contigs into restriction fragments, chimeric contigs were broken into non-chimeric parts thereby correcting the assembly errors mentioned above.
evidence: This describes a feature of the GRAAL algorithm.

claim: 3D signals from meta3C data can be used to annotate centromeres of unknown species.
source: For instance, interchromosomal signals corresponding to centromere clustering were clearly visible in the matrix, emphasizing that 3D signals could also be used to annotate the centromeres of unknown species isolated from meta3C data (Figure 2F; Figure 2—figure supplement 4B; Marie-Nelly et al., 2014b).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the visible centromere clustering signals in the contact maps.

claim: The environmental sediment sample was enriched for prokaryotic organisms by cultivating for 14 hr in Luria broth and filtrating prior to meta3C library construction.
source: Because environmental genomes usually contain a tremendous diversity of species, including many eukaryotes of large genome sizes, we decided to enrich our sample for prokaryotic organisms by cultivating it for 14 hr in Luria broth and filtrating it prior to meta3C library construction and sequencing.
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure for the environmental sample.

claim: The Louvain algorithm identified 184 significant communities from the environmental sediment meta3C assembly, with a total size of 111 Mb and median size of 300 kb.
source: Contigs generated from the meta3C sediment library were clustered using the Louvain algorithm, yielding 184 significant communities (total size 111 Mb, median size 300 kb, with 19 communities containing more than 1 Mb).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the clustering analysis.

claim: For each community in the environmental sample, more than 80% of the genes identified by MG-RAST were attributed to the same taxonomic class.
source: Each community was analyzed using MG-RAST (Glass et al., 2010), showing relatively homogeneous taxonomic compositions in most communities (Figure 3—figure supplement 1). For each community, more than 80% of the genes identified by MG-RAST within the contigs were attributed to the same taxonomic class.
evidence: This demonstrates the taxonomic homogeneity of the identified communities.

claim: At the family level, 8 out of the 11 largest communities from the environmental sample were >80% homogeneous.
source: Going down to family level, 8 out of the 11 largest communities were >80% homogeneous, with the remaining three presenting more complex patterns that will require further investigation and development.
evidence: This is a quantitative assessment of taxonomic homogeneity at the family level.

claim: One community from the environmental sample contained contigs covering 95% of the V. cholerae genome control.
source: One community was composed of contigs covering 95% of the V. cholerae genome control (for a total amount of 3.9 Mb congruent with the expected size of the genome; Figure 3B, i), confirming the ability of this approach to pool DNA regions according to their genome of origin.
evidence: This validates the approach using the V. cholerae control added to the environmental sample.

claim: Communities from the environmental sample contained contigs belonging to Aeromonas veronii (4 Mb, 72% of reference) and Exiguobacterium sp. (3.1 Mb, 36% of reference).
source: Other communities contained contigs belonging to other discrete species, related for instance to the ubiquitous bacteria Aeromonas veronii or Exiguobacterium sp. (for total amounts of 4 Mb and 3.1 Mb, aligning to 72% and 36% of the reference genomes of 4.5 Mb and 3 Mb total sizes, respectively; Figure 3B, i).
evidence: This demonstrates the identification of specific bacterial species from the environmental sample.

claim: Plasmids annotated as belonging to Bacillus megaterium were retrieved almost entirely within a single Bacilli community in the environmental sample.
source: In this study, plasmids annotated as belonging to Bacillus megaterium were retrieved almost entirely within a single Bacilli community (Figure 3B, ii), suggesting that this community presented indeed a relatively homogeneous content and therefore validating our approach.
evidence: This validates the approach by showing that plasmids cluster with their expected host genome.

claim: The 3D structure of the A. veronii-related community from the environmental sample is reminiscent of those of B. subtilis and C. crescentus.
source: Although the limited sequencing depth of our experiment restrained our ability to scaffold optimally the contigs of the communities using GRAAL, mapping the reads present in the community related to A. veronii against the reference genome of this species revealed a 3D structure reminiscent of those of B. subtilis and C. crescentus (Figure 3C; Animation 12).
evidence: This is observed by comparing the 3D structure to those of other bacteria.

claim: The average organization of yeast genomes differs radically from those of bacterial nucleoids because of contrasted replication and division processes and timings.
source: The average organization of yeast genomes was found to differ radically from those of bacterial nucleoids, most likely because of contrasted replication and division processes and timings.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the observed differences in chromosome organization.

claim: In Saccharomycetes, most of the chromosome organization is driven by the clustering of centromeres at the spindle pole body, which remains prominent throughout most of the cell cycle during exponential growth.
source: Most of the organization in Saccharomycetes appears driven by the clustering of the centromeres at the spindle pole body; this clustering remains the prominent structural feature throughout most of the cell cycle (i.e., G1 + S phase + G2) during exponential growth, with mitosis representing only a fraction of the cycle.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the observed Rabl configuration in yeast genomes.

claim: Meta3C differs from previous approaches by using a single library for generating contigs, binning them, scaffolding them, and revealing the 3D structure of corresponding species through blind analysis.
source: Our approach conveniently uses a single meta3C library and a blind analysis for generating contigs, binning them, scaffolding them, and revealing the 3D structure of the corresponding species.
evidence: This describes a key distinguishing feature of the meta3C approach compared to other methods.

claim: The meta3C blind analysis allows delineating communities without prior knowledge of the number of species present in the mix.
source: Besides, our blind analysis allowed us to delineate communities without prior knowledge of the number of species present in the mix; this contrasts with the approach of Burton et al. (2014), which apparently requires such prior knowledge.
evidence: This describes an advantage of the meta3C approach over other methods.

claim: Meta3C generates de novo chromosome scaffolds without assumptions regarding the number of chromosomes present in the mixture.
source: Similarly, we generate de novo chromosome scaffolds without any assumptions regarding the number of chromosomes present in the mixture, a realistic approach when it comes to exploring environmental samples or complete the assembly of complex genomes.
evidence: This describes another advantage of the meta3C approach.

claim: The adequacy between the cross-linking step and the restriction step is essential for the recovery of long-distance cis contacts that improve de novo genome scaffolding and reveal 3D structure.
source: Furthermore, our experience with the analysis of chromosome organization in both bacteria and yeast species emphasized the importance of the initial steps for the success of such experiment. The adequacy between the cross-linking step, which depends on the incubation time and the concentration of the fixating agent, and the restriction step and choice of the restriction enzyme, is essential for the recovery of long-distance cis contacts that improve de novo genome scaffolding and, importantly, reveal the 3D structure.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental experience described in the study.

claim: Meta3C protocol does not involve an enrichment step for religated fragments, unlike the Hi-C protocol.
source: This relatively high percentage results from the fact that, unlike the Hi-C protocol (Lieberman-Aiden et al., 2009), meta3C does not involve an enrichment step for religated fragments ('Materials and methods').
evidence: This describes a methodological difference between meta3C and Hi-C.

claim: The contact frequency between two chromosomal segments obeys to some extent the laws of polymer physics.
source: The frequency with which two chromosomal segments come in contact, as measured in genome-wide chromosome conformation capture (3C) experiments (Dekker et al., 2002; Lieberman-Aiden et al., 2009), obeys to some extent the laws of polymer physics (Rippe, 2001; Wong et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to literature on polymer physics and 3C experiments.

claim: Contact frequencies can be used to identify synteny between DNA segments up to a few 100s kilobases apart.
source: Contact frequencies can be used to identify synteny between DNA segments up to a few 100s kilobases (kb) apart, and two studies recently applied this concept to refining the human genome sequence (Burton et al., 2013; Kaplan and Dekker, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies that applied this concept to the human genome.

claim: GRAAL is a robust and explicit statistical method for using chromosomal contact data to generate precise scaffolds of genomes at the highest resolution possible.
source: Using chromosomal contacts data in order to generate the precise scaffold of a given genome is however a difficult task: hence, we developed GRAAL, a robust and explicit statistical method to tackle this issue at the highest resolution possible (Marie-Nelly et al., 2014a; Figure 1A).
evidence: This describes the GRAAL method developed by the authors.

claim: If interactions between chromosomes within a nucleus can be resolved, then it is possible to resolve chromosomes of various species mixed together.
source: Since this approach enables the identification of individual chromosomes within the same nuclei, we hypothesized that tridimensional (3D) organization holds enough specific information to distinguish as well DNA segments of chromosomes present within different organisms (Figure 1A). In other words, if the interactions between chromosomes contained within a human or a fungal nucleus can be resolved, then it may be possible to resolve the chromosomes of various species mixed together.
evidence: This is the central hypothesis of the meta3C approach, which is then validated experimentally.

claim: The two chromosomes of V. cholerae exhibit higher contact frequencies with each other than with chromosomes of other species.
source: As in a typical 3C experiment squares appeared on the diagonal of the matrix, revealing individual chromosomes: the circular chromosomes of both E. coli and B. subtilis were recovered as separate entities, whereas the two chromosomes of V. cholerae yielded two squares exhibiting higher contact frequencies with each other than with the chromosomes of the other species—as expected since these chromosomes share the same cellular compartment (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is observed in the contact map and expected based on the fact that both chromosomes are in the same cell.

claim: The duplication in the E. coli genome has an IS2 element at one boundary (coord. 390,063) and an IS3 element within it.
source: A correlation analysis of the contacts between these two regions of interest (a chromosome region encompassing the duplication and the plasmid) revealed clearly that, on the one hand, a copy of the duplication is in close contact with the plasmid (with an IS2 at one the boundaries [coord. 390,063] and an IS3 within), and that on the other hand the plasmid contacts with the E. coli genome drop sharply past the duplication boundaries, in agreement with an integration of one copy of the duplication within a F' plasmid (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is determined through correlation analysis of contact frequencies.

claim: The duplication breakpoints in the E. coli genome are at coordinates ~240,000:380,000 along the chromosome.
source: This analysis allowed to position duplication breakpoints at coordinates ∼240,000:380,000 along the chromosome.
evidence: This is determined through correlation analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Chromosome 1 of V. cholerae exhibits a more 'open' configuration while chromosome 2 has paired replichores.
source: The two chromosomes of V. cholera were found in two different conformations, with chromosome 1 exhibiting a more 'open' configuration and the replichores of chromosome 2 appearing paired (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is observed in the 3D reconstruction shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Interchromosomal contacts in V. cholerae do not span the entire length of chromosome 1 but start between the Ori macrodomain of chromosome 2 and positions at about one-third of chromosome 1 arms.
source: Interchromosomal contacts did not span the entire length of chromosome 1 but started between the Ori macrodomain of chromosome 2 and positions located at about one-third of chromosome 1 arms (black dotted squares, Figure 1D).
evidence: This is observed in the contact map shown in Figure 1D.

claim: V. cholerae chromosome I initiates replication first whereas chromosome II starts to replicate later.
source: Whereas the two Ter regions appeared of the same color, consistent with the fact that both chromosomes I and II achieve replication synchronously (Rasmussen et al., 2007), the Ori regions presented, as expected, different coverages: chromosome I initiates replication first whereas chromosome II starts only to replicate later.
evidence: This is inferred from read coverage data representing replication timing.

claim: The de novo assembly of the three bacterial genomes from meta3C data had only 0.7% chimeric contigs (17 out of 2436 contigs, 52,373 bp total).
source: Only 17 out of the 2436 contigs were chimeric (0.7%), accounting for 52,373 bp in total (0.4% of the total size of the assembly).
evidence: This is a quantitative assessment of assembly quality from the Materials and methods section.

claim: The low number of chimeric contigs in the bacterial assembly results from the limited number of species in the mix and their low repeat content.
source: This relatively low number probably results from the limited number of species contained in the mix and their low repeat content. It also shows that chimeric religation during the experiment introduces little background interactions in the assembly process.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the low chimeric contig rate.

claim: Chimeric religation during the meta3C experiment introduces little background interactions in the assembly process.
source: This relatively low number probably results from the limited number of species contained in the mix and their low repeat content. It also shows that chimeric religation during the experiment introduces little background interactions in the assembly process.
evidence: This is concluded from the low rate of chimeric contigs in the bacterial assembly.

claim: The yeast meta3C assembly had 9,599 chimeric contigs representing 27.1% of the total number of contigs.
source: In contrast to the previous results on the bacterial meta3C assembly, there were 9,599 chimeric contigs in the yeast case, representing 27.1% of the total number of contigs.
evidence: This is a quantitative assessment from the Materials and methods section.

claim: Chimeric contigs arise when dealing with mixtures of repeat-rich genomes because near-identical repeats are found in different genomes in the mixture.
source: This shows that chimeric contigs arise when dealing with mixtures of repeat-rich genomes, likely because near-identical repeats (such as transposable elements) are found in different genomes in the mixture.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the high chimeric contig rate in the yeast assembly.

claim: Assembly mistakes from near-identical repeats can be avoided by using longer reads or resolved a posteriori using GRAAL.
source: Such assembly mistakes will be probably avoided if using longer reads (since repeats longer than the read length pose problem during assembly) or, alternatively, can be resolved a posteriori using GRAAL.
evidence: This is a suggestion for improving assembly quality based on understanding of the problem.

claim: After GRAAL processing of S. bayanus contigs, the N50 length reached 190,514 bp and 77% of the total length was assembled into regions larger than 50 kb.
source: We used GRAAL to reassemble the 2,060 contigs (N50 = 16,764 bp) contained in the S. bayanus community identified by the Louvain algorithm. The resulting scaffolding showed a large improvement for all assembly parameters. The N50 length now reached 190,514 bp, and 77% of the total length of the assembly was assembled into regions larger than 50 kb (as compared to 3% before running the software).
evidence: This demonstrates the improvement achieved by GRAAL scaffolding.

claim: After GRAAL processing of N. castellii contigs, the N50 length reached 792,652 bp and 96% of the assembled data was in scaffolds larger than 50 kb.
source: The result was even more spectacular for N. castellii (probably due to its higher coverage in the meta3C library): after running GRAAL on the 999 contigs (N50 = 27,452 bp) in the community delineated by the Louvain algorithm, N50 length reached 792,652 bp, and 96% of the assembled data was in scaffolds larger than 50 kb (with 11 scaffolds covering 95% of the 10 chromosomes).
evidence: This demonstrates the dramatic improvement achieved by GRAAL scaffolding for N. castellii.

claim: The environmental sediment meta3C assembly generated 130,713 contigs with N50 = 1,274 kb and total length = 111 Mb.
source: 67,920,671 pairs of reads (91 bp useful) were used to assemble the raw culture from the river sediment. As a positive assembly control, 500,000 reads from a 3C library of V. cholerae were added into this pool of sequences. The assembly generated 130,713 contigs (2,250 > 5 kb, N50 = 1,274 kb, total length = 111 Mb).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the environmental sample assembly.

claim: After realignment of reads to the environmental sediment contigs, approximately 62% of reads could be mapped.
source: After realignment of the initial reads along the generated contig, 42,705,64 PE reads could be mapped against the assembled contigs (∼62%).
evidence: This is a quantitative measure of assembly quality for the environmental sample.

claim: Mitochondrial genomes behave as separate entities in meta3C experiments.
source: Figure 2—figure supplement 1.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 which demonstrates mitochondrial genomes as separate entities.

claim: Chromosome 3 of N. castellii was split into two scaffolds because of the presence of the large, unassembled rDNA array on this chromosome.
source: Overall these 11 scaffolds covered 94.5% of the reference sequence of the 10 chromosomes (chromosome 3 was split into two scaffolds because of the presence of the large, unassembled rDNA array on this chromosome), illustrating the ability of this de novo analysis to correctly assemble and scaffold unknown genomes (see Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This explains why 11 scaffolds were obtained for 10 chromosomes.
